title: CCST Cybersecurity (100-160) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from Cisco's public 100-160 CCST Cybersecurity objective domains (checked 2026-11-26). Not real exam questions. Cisco doesn't publish the number of items or the topic weights, so this is a 45-item stand-in that fits the real 50 minutes, with an even split across the five domains and 4 hands-on items.

q.q: A coworker's laptop runs an old version of a PDF reader with a known flaw. A criminal group is sending phishing mail to the unit. In risk terms, what is the old PDF reader?
o: A vulnerability, a weakness that could be used against it
Right. The flaw is the weakness. The criminal group is the threat, and the code that abuses the flaw is the exploit.
A threat, because it is the thing most likely to cause harm to the unit's mission and data
A threat is the actor or event that could do harm, such as the criminal group. The reader is only the weak spot.
An exploit, because it is the code or method that attacks the laptop from the outside
An exploit is the tool or method that abuses a weakness. The reader is not attacking anything.
A risk, because it is the chance of loss to the unit
Risk is the chance and impact of a loss when a threat meets a weakness. It is not the software itself.

q.q: A technician changes the dose figures in a clinic's patient database. Staff can still open the database and nobody outside the clinic saw the data. Which part of the CIA triad was broken?
o: Confidentiality, because the data was exposed to outsiders
Confidentiality covers who can read data. The story says nobody outside saw it.
Availability, because staff lost access to the database during the change
Staff could still open the database, so it stayed available.
Integrity, since the data was changed without permission
Right. Integrity means data stays accurate and unaltered. Wrong doses are a loss of integrity, even though nothing leaked.
Accountability, because the change was not logged anywhere
Logging is an accounting control. It is not one of the three CIA goals.

q.q: While helping with an authorized task on a shared drive, you find a folder of coworkers' pay records open to everyone. What fits a security code of ethics?
o: Read a few files to confirm the exposure is real before you decide whether to tell anyone
Reading private records goes past what you were authorized to do, even with good intentions.
Tell the data owner or the security office, and leave the files unread
Right. Reporting the problem and leaving the data alone follows the ethics of trust and need to know.
Fix the permissions on the folder yourself and say nothing, so nobody blames the owner
Hiding a problem keeps the owner from learning about a possible exposure that others may have already used.
Post a warning in the unit chat so everyone can see how bad it is
This spreads word of the open folder and can make the exposure worse before it is fixed.

q.q: The phone rings. The caller says they are from IT support, sounds rushed, and asks you to read out the six-digit code your authenticator app just showed. What kind of attack is this?
o: Spear phishing, a message written for one chosen target
Spear phishing is usually an email or message aimed at one person or group. This attack is a live voice call.
Smishing, a text message that pushes you to tap a link or reply
Smishing arrives by SMS or chat text. This attack came by voice.
Pretexting by email, where the attacker builds a false story in a written message to the unit
Pretexting means a made-up story, but here it was told on a call, not in an email.
Vishing, a phone call that tricks you into giving up a secret
Right. Voice phishing uses a phone call and urgency to get codes or passwords.

q.q: A text says your parcel is held and asks you to tap a link and enter your date of birth. Which is the best response?
o: Tap the link on a locked-down phone, but enter nothing
Opening the link can already run a bad page or download something harmful.
Reply STOP so the sender removes your number from the list
A reply confirms your number is live and gives the sender more to work with.
Forward the text to coworkers to warn them about the scam
Forwarding the live link invites coworkers to tap it. Report it to security instead.
Don't tap the link. Report it as smishing, then delete it
Right. A text with a link and a data request is smishing. Delete it and report it.

q.q: Which TWO facts make Internet of Things (IoT) devices, such as cameras, a common weak point? (Choose two.)
o: Firmware is often old and rarely updated
Right. Without a patch process, known flaws stay open for years.
Many ship with default or hard-coded passwords
Right. Attackers scan for the same factory logins on thousands of devices.
They never connect to a network, so nobody can reach them
Most IoT devices exist to be on the network. That is how they get attacked.
They always run a full antivirus agent that blocks malware
Small devices usually cannot run security agents.
Their traffic is always encrypted end to end by default
Many send data in plain text unless somebody turns encryption on.

q.q: Security staff find a group that has lived quietly in a defense contractor's network for eight months, moving from system to system and slowly copying design files. Which term fits best?
o: Advanced persistent threat (APT), a long, quiet intrusion
Right. An APT is a skilled group that stays hidden for a long time to reach a goal such as stealing data.
A targeted ransomware campaign against the contractor
Ransomware locks files and demands payment. It makes noise. This group wanted to stay hidden.
An insider threat from one employee who copies files slowly
An insider is a person who already has access. The story describes a group that moved from system to system.
A botnet that uses the contractor's servers to send spam
A botnet is a group of infected machines under one controller. It is a tool, not this quiet, targeted intrusion.

q.q: A switch records that admin account ops7 typed "no ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.1" at 14:02. Which part of AAA is this record?
o: Authentication, which proves who the user is when they log in to the switch
Authentication is the login step, such as a password check.
Accounting, which records what a logged-in user did
Right. Accounting keeps a trail of actions and times.
Authorization, which decides what the user is allowed to do on the device
Authorization sets the allowed commands. The record here shows what was actually done.
Availability, which keeps the device reachable
Availability is a CIA goal, not part of AAA.

q.q: A unit has 30 switches and a Wi-Fi network. It wants every administrator to log in with one central account list, with logins logged in one place. Which technology fits?
o: Local accounts created separately on each of the 30 switches
This leaves 30 separate lists to manage, with no central log.
MAC address filtering on every access point and switch port
MAC filtering checks a device, not a person, and it is easy to bypass.
A RADIUS server that approves each login
Right. RADIUS centralizes authentication and accounting for network access, so one account works on every device.
A shared admin password kept in a locked binder
A shared secret hides who did what and cannot be revoked for one person.

q.q: Which TWO choices form true multifactor authentication for a laptop login? (Choose two answers that together make two different factors.)
o: A second password typed after the first
Two passwords are still the same factor, something you know.
A PIN the user knows (something you know)
Right. A PIN is a knowledge factor. Paired with the card, it makes two different factors.
A smart card the user holds (something you have)
Right. A card is a possession factor.
The same password typed on a second screen
Typing the same secret twice adds no new factor.
A security question such as a pet's name
This is also something you know, and the answer is often easy to find.

q.q: A laptop holding a trouble-ticket export is stolen from a car. Which control best protects the data while the laptop sits powered off?
o: Full-disk encryption, for data at rest
Right. Encrypted drives stay unreadable without the key.
A TLS connection to the ticket website while the export is downloaded
TLS protects data in transit while it moves. It does nothing for a stored export.
A hash of each file kept on the same laptop
A hash shows if a file changed. It does not hide the contents.
A screen lock timer set to one minute, plus a BIOS password
A lock screen does not stop someone from reading the drive after removing it.

q.q: A browser shows a padlock for a web page. What makes the browser trust the site's certificate?
o: The site owner states, in a banner on the page, that the site is safe and fully trusted
Any site can claim that. Trust comes from a verifiable signature.
It was signed by a CA the browser already trusts
Right. In public key infrastructure (PKI), trust comes from a signature chain back to a trusted certificate authority (CA).
The certificate's name matches the web address the user typed
A matching name is checked, but anyone can make a certificate with any name. The trusted signature is what counts.
The page opens over port 443 with a padlock already on the tab
The padlock is the result of the checks, not the cause of trust.

q.q: Which TWO algorithms are considered weak and should not be chosen for new systems? (Choose two.)
o: SHA-256
SHA-256 is a strong hash and is in wide use.
AES with a 256-bit key
AES-256 is a strong, widely used cipher.
RSA with a 3072-bit key
This key size is considered strong today.
DES
Right. DES has a 56-bit key and can be broken with modern hardware.
MD5
Right. MD5 has known collision attacks, so it is not safe for integrity checks or signatures.

q.q: You download an installer from a mirror site. The publisher lists its SHA-256 hash on its own official site. Your computed hash matches. What does the match show?
o: The file is free of malware, because a hash works like an antivirus scan of its contents
A hash cannot judge safety. It only compares bytes.
The file is encrypted, because hashing hides the contents
Hashing is one-way and does not encrypt the file.
The file's publisher is verified, because the same hash is on the download page
A hash on the same page as the download proves nothing about who made it. Only a trusted source for the hash helps.
The file is the same one the publisher hashed, so it was not changed on the way
Right. A matching hash from a trusted source shows integrity.

q.q: A LAN user finds that traffic to the default gateway is being sent to another host's MAC address. Replies to ARP requests were forged. What is the attacker setting up?
o: A SYN flood against the gateway to fill its connection table
A SYN flood uses half-open TCP connections. It does not change MAC mappings.
A DNS cache poisoning attack that changes the answers the resolver gives to every client
This targets name answers. The scenario describes address mapping on the LAN.
A man-in-the-middle position to read or alter traffic
Right. ARP has no authentication, so a forged reply can steer a victim's traffic through the attacker.
An ICMP echo test of the gateway
Pings test reachability. They do not redirect traffic.

q.q: A web server slows to a crawl. Its connection table is full of entries in the SYN_RECEIVED state from thousands of different source addresses, and none of them finish the handshake. Which attack is this?
o: An ARP spoofing attack aimed at the web server's MAC address
ARP spoofing redirects traffic. It does not fill the connection table.
A rogue DHCP server handing out leases from many addresses
DHCP attacks affect addressing, not half-open TCP sessions.
A TCP SYN flood, a denial of service
Right. The attacker never completes the three-way handshake, so half-open connections fill the table.
A UDP broadcast storm from one looping switch port
The signs are TCP handshake states, not UDP broadcasts.

q.q: A new laptop on the guest network gets an address, but its default gateway is 10.9.9.9, which is not your router. DNS also points to that host. What is the most likely cause?
o: The laptop's MAC address is longer than the network allows
MAC addresses have a fixed length and don't affect the gateway.
A rogue DHCP server, a fake one that answered first
Right. A false DHCP server can hand out its own gateway and DNS to steer traffic.
The router's ICMP replies are disabled, so the gateway looks wrong
This would affect ping replies, not the address that DHCP hands out.
The web server's TLS certificate expired last month on the main site
A certificate problem cannot change the gateway a device is given.

q.q: A branch network uses 192.168.40.0/27. How many usable host addresses are in that subnet?
o: 32 is the total, which includes the network and broadcast addresses.
62 is the host count of a /26, one bit shorter.
14 is the host count of a /28, one bit longer.
Right. A /27 has 32 addresses. Subtract the network and broadcast addresses and 30 are left for hosts.

q.q: Which of these is a private IPv4 address that a router would not route on the public Internet?
o: The 172 private range ends at 172.31.255.255, so this one is public.
The private range is 192.168.x.x. This is a public address.
This is shared address space used by some providers. It is not one of the private ranges.

q.q: A unit hosts a public web page and also keeps staff file servers. Where should the public web server be placed?
o: On the same inside network as the staff file servers and the printers
A break-in at the web server would then give a clear path to internal data.
Outside the firewall, directly on the Internet
With no firewall in front, nothing filters traffic to it.
In a DMZ, a segment behind the firewall but apart from the inside network
Right. If the web server is attacked, the inside network remains behind a second barrier.
On the guest Wi-Fi network next to visitors' phones
Guest devices are untrusted. Putting servers there creates its own risk.

q.q: A security team places a decoy server with fake files and no real users. Any connection to it raises an alert. What is this decoy called?
o: A proxy server
A proxy forwards requests for clients. It is not bait.
A honeypot
Right. A honeypot is bait that shows attacker activity early and draws attention away from real systems.
A jump host
A jump host is a hardened stepping-stone for admins. It is a real system, not bait.
A load balancer
A load balancer spreads traffic across real servers.

q.q: What is the main difference between an IDS and an IPS?
o: An IPS sits inline and can block traffic, while an IDS watches and alerts
Right. Inline placement lets an IPS drop packets. An IDS usually watches a copy of the traffic.
An IDS encrypts the traffic it inspects, while an IPS only reads it
Neither device encrypts traffic. Both inspect it.
An IDS works only in cloud networks, while an IPS works only on a single on-site network
Both can be deployed on-site, in virtual form or in the cloud.
An IPS works on stored logs only, while an IDS works on live traffic and can drop packets
An IPS inspects live traffic inline. The statement turns the roles around.

q.q: Which setting gives a small office the strongest protection for its Wi-Fi?
o: WEP with a long key
WEP is broken and can be cracked in minutes.
An open network with a hidden SSID
No encryption means anyone can read the traffic.
WPA with TKIP and a short passphrase
TKIP is outdated and a short passphrase is easy to guess.
WPA3-Personal with a long passphrase
Right. WPA3 gives the strongest encryption of the options, and a long passphrase resists guessing.

q.q: Which TWO statements about hiding the SSID and using MAC address filtering on a small-office network are true? (Choose two.)
o: MAC filtering makes WPA encryption unnecessary
Filtering controls who joins, not how traffic is protected.
MAC filtering can be bypassed by copying an allowed address
Right. MAC addresses are sent in the clear, so an attacker can learn and spoof one.
Both settings stop an attacker with a packet capture tool
Both are weak and easy to see through.
A hidden SSID encrypts the wireless traffic
Hiding the name does not encrypt anything.
A hidden SSID can still be seen by tools when a client connects
Right. The name appears in frames from clients, so hiding it does not stop a determined person.

q.q: A router ACL has these rules in order: 10 permit ip any any, 20 deny tcp any any eq 23 (Telnet). A user tries to Telnet through the router. What happens?
o: The packet is permitted, because rule 10 matches first
Right. ACLs are read top to bottom and the first match wins, so rule 20 is never reached.
The packet is denied, because deny rules always win
Order decides, not rule type. Rule 10 matches before the deny.
The packet is dropped, because Telnet is encrypted
Telnet is not encrypted, and nothing here drops it.
The router picks the longer rule and denies the packet
ACLs do not choose by length. They use the first match.

q.q: A worker at a hotel connects to the unit's network from her laptop. Which technology keeps her traffic private on the hotel Wi-Fi?
o: A hidden SSID on the hotel's guest Wi-Fi network, which she does not control
The hotel's Wi-Fi settings are not under her control and don't protect her traffic.
A MAC filter set on the hotel's access point by the front desk
MAC filtering is an access setting and does not encrypt traffic.
A honeypot placed on the hotel network by the unit's staff
A decoy is not a privacy tool for her traffic.
A VPN tunnel from the laptop to the unit's VPN gateway
Right. A VPN encrypts the traffic between the laptop and the gateway.

q.q: A laptop connects to the wired network but its antivirus is out of date. The network moves it into a limited VLAN until it is updated. Which technology does this?
o: A honeypot, which lures attackers to fake systems and records what they do
A honeypot is bait. It does not check devices.
A forward proxy, which relays web requests for users and can filter the sites they visit
A proxy does not decide which VLAN a device uses.
Network access control (NAC), which checks device health first
Right. NAC checks posture and can quarantine devices that fail.
A hash check, which verifies the integrity of each file
A hash does not measure device health.

q.q: On a Linux server, "ls -l" shows "-rwxr-x---  1 maria ops  report.sh". A user named bob is not maria and is not in the group ops. What can bob do with this file?
o: Read and run it, because the file has the executable bit set for someone
The execute bit applies only to the owner and the group here.
Nothing, since the permissions for others are ---
Right. The three groups of letters are owner, group and others. Others have no rights.
Read it only, because group members can read it and bob is a regular user
Bob is not in the group, so the group rights do not apply.
Change it, because bob can use sudo
Having sudo is a separate matter. By the file's own permissions, bob has no access.

q.q: A standard user runs a script that abuses an unpatched service and ends up with SYSTEM rights on a Windows server. What is this called?
o: Lateral movement from the server to another host
Lateral movement means going from one machine to another. Here the user raised rights on the same server.
Privilege escalation, gaining rights beyond those granted
Right. The user gained higher rights than they were given.
Credential stuffing against the server's login page
Credential stuffing reuses stolen passwords. Here a service flaw was abused.
Session hijacking of an administrator's browser
Hijacking steals a live session. Nothing here involves an admin's session.

q.q: Which TWO actions harden a new Windows or Linux server? (Choose two.)
o: Leave the guest account on in case someone needs it
An unused account is an open door.
Disable the host firewall to keep troubleshooting simple
Turning off the firewall removes a layer of protection.
Change or remove default accounts and passwords
Right. Default logins are the first thing attackers try.
Turn off services and features the server does not need
Right. Fewer running services mean fewer ways in.
Give all staff local administrator rights to save time
This widens the damage if any account is lost.

q.q: You are authorized to check one workstation that may be talking to a suspicious address. Which command shows its current network connections, with the program that owns each?
o: nslookup with the host's name, run against the workstation itself
nslookup turns names into IP addresses. It does not list connections.
tcpdump capturing all traffic on the network card for ten minutes
tcpdump captures packets. It does not show which program owns a connection.
ping to the suspicious address, repeated until it answers
Ping tests reachability. It does not list connections on the host.
netstat with the option that shows the owning process
Right. netstat lists connections and listening ports, and process options show which program owns them.

q.q: On a host you are authorized to monitor, you need to capture only the DNS traffic to and from 10.1.1.20. Which command fits?
o: nslookup 10.1.1.20 port 53, run on the host
nslookup is a single query tool, not a packet capture.
netstat -an | find "10.1.1.20:53", run every few seconds
This shows current sockets, not captured packets.
tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.1.1.20 and port 53
Right. It sets the interface and filters by address and DNS port.
tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100 port 80 and host 10.1.1.20
Port 80 is web traffic, not DNS.

q.q: An audit finds a server that no one remembers installing and that has never been patched. Which practice would most likely have prevented this?
o: Keeping a current hardware and software inventory
Right. You can only patch and secure devices you know exist.
Using a longer Wi-Fi passphrase and changing it every week
This does nothing about forgotten servers.
Encrypting every backup tape before it leaves the building
Encryption protects data but doesn't reveal unknown systems.
Running a monthly phishing test for all staff
Phishing tests train people. They don't find forgotten servers.

q.q: A unit lets staff read work email on their own phones (BYOD). Which control best protects unit data on those phones?
o: A reminder email asking staff to be careful with work messages
A reminder is not a technical control.
Allowing any app to be installed as long as staff say it is safe
Unvetted apps raise the chance of data leaks.
A mobile device management (MDM) policy with encryption and remote wipe
Right. MDM can require encryption and a passcode, and remove unit data if the phone is lost.
A rule that personal phones may connect only to the guest Wi-Fi network at the unit's offices
The network alone doesn't protect data that sits on the phone.

q.q: A monthly operating system update is ready for 500 workstations. What is the best deployment approach?
o: Push it to a small pilot group first, then roll out in stages
Right. A pilot finds problems early, and stages limit the damage.
Push it to everyone at once, since the vendor tested it
Vendor tests can't cover every unit configuration.
Skip it unless a coworker reports a problem with the old version
Waiting leaves known flaws open.
Install it only on the machines whose users complain about problems with their computers
Complaints are not a reliable sign of which systems have missing patches.

q.q: Why should staff apply firmware updates to routers and printers, not just operating system updates?
o: Firmware updates only add features, so security fixes can wait until the next model
Firmware updates often fix real security flaws.
Firmware does not matter once a device has a strong password
Passwords don't fix a flaw in the code itself.
Windows Update downloads and installs router and printer firmware automatically for every device
Windows Update handles Windows and its drivers, not an unrelated device's firmware.
Firmware flaws can be exploited, and OS patches don't fix the device's own software
Right. Network devices run their own software that has to be patched separately.

q.q: In the Windows Security log, Event Viewer shows 300 events with ID 4625 (failed logon) for the account "administrator" from one IP in five minutes. What does it most likely show?
o: A normal scheduled backup job that signs in with a service account
A backup would show successful service logons, not hundreds of failures.
A password-guessing attempt against the account
Right. Many failed logons in a short time from one source is a classic brute-force pattern.
A user who forgot the password and keeps retrying it from one PC
One person's retries rarely reach 300 in five minutes, and they would stop at the lockout limit.
A successful software update
Updates do not generate failed logon events like these.

q.q: Which log entry most deserves a closer look from a junior analyst?
o: A scheduled backup completed at 02:00 without any errors and with a normal size
This is expected and routine.
The Security audit log was cleared by a user account at 03:12
Right. Clearing logs is a common step to hide activity. It should be checked right away.
A DHCP lease was renewed for a workstation in the finance office
Lease renewals happen all day.
The print spooler service started automatically after a reboot
Services start normally after a reboot.

q.q: An antivirus scan finds ransomware-like files on one office PC, and that PC still has its network cable plugged in. What should the technician do first?
o: Leave it connected and run a full scan so the antivirus can pull new signatures
Reconnecting before the cause is known risks spreading the malware.
Keep it connected and start a scan of the shared drive so the scan finishes faster
Scanning while connected lets the malware reach the share.
Disconnect it from the network, so it can't spread
Right. Isolation limits spread and keeps the machine available for study.
Reboot it several times to see if the files go away
Rebooting does not remove malware and may trigger it.

q.q: A scan report shows: Quarantined 3, Failed to clean 2 (file in use). What is the best next step?
o: Run an offline or safe-mode scan, then re-scan
Right. Files in use can't be cleaned while running, so scan again from safe mode and verify.
Mark the PC clean, since most files were quarantined
Two items were not cleaned, so the infection may remain.
Delete the quarantine folder to save disk space and rescan only the remaining files
The quarantine folder holds the evidence and the isolated threats.
Give the user local admin rights so the scan can finish without stopping
More rights for the user don't fix files in use, and they raise risk.

q.q: A tester reads a company's public job postings and archived web pages to learn what systems it runs, without contacting the company's own systems at all. What kind of reconnaissance is this?
o: Active reconnaissance
Active recon sends traffic to the target, such as scanning ports.
A vulnerability scan
A scan sends probes to the target. No probes were sent here.
Penetration testing
A pen test goes further and tries to break in, and needs written scope.
Passive reconnaissance
Right. Using public information without touching the target is passive.

q.q: A junior analyst wants to run a port scan against the unit's file servers to find open services. What must be in place first?
o: Nothing, because a scan only reads and never changes anything
Scans can disrupt systems and are treated as attack activity without permission.
Verbal approval from a coworker on the next shift
Coworkers don't own the systems, and a verbal OK leaves no record.
A VPN connection to hide where the scan comes from and keep the owner from noticing
Hiding the source is no authorization and looks suspicious.
Written permission from the system owner with a scope and time
Right. Scanning systems you do not own without permission can be illegal, and written approval protects you.

q.q: Why do teams schedule automated vulnerability scans, such as weekly runs, instead of only scanning by hand once a year?
o: Automated scans remove the need to fix anything afterward
A scan only finds problems. People still have to fix them.
Automated scans never produce false positives, so no review is needed
They still can, so results need review.
New flaws and changes show up between reviews, so regular scans find them sooner and more consistently
Right. Frequent and repeatable scans keep up with new vulnerabilities and system changes.
Scheduled scans are required by law, so the unit does not need any other security controls
Scans don't replace a firewall or any other control.

q.q: What is a CVE entry?
o: A severity score from 0 to 10 for the flaw
The score is a CVSS value. A CVE is the ID of the flaw.
A public identifier for one known vulnerability
Right. A CVE ID names one flaw so everyone can talk about the same issue.
A patch released by the software vendor to fix the flaw
A patch fixes a flaw. A CVE only names it.
A scanner that finds flaws on the network and writes an automatic report
A scanner is a tool. A CVE is a catalog entry.

q.q: What is one limit of relying only on a vulnerability database to find your risks?
o: It lists only known flaws, so it can't warn about unknown ones such as zero-day flaws
Right. If a flaw isn't published yet, it won't be in the database.
It is always updated too slowly to be useful for any current security decision
Databases are often updated daily and are very useful.
It only covers flaws in printers and other office hardware
Databases cover many types of software and hardware.
It blocks the traffic of any system it lists as vulnerable
A database is a reference, not a security device.

q.q: During an incident, which TWO practices keep communication and documentation healthy? (Choose two.)
o: Keep notes on a personal phone so they stay handy
Personal devices are not controlled storage for incident records.
Send stakeholders regular updates before, during and after the incident
Right. Short, steady updates avoid surprises and rumors.
Wait until the incident is closed before telling anyone
Silence leaves managers and users guessing, and delays decisions.
Post all technical details in a public chat for transparency
Public posting can leak sensitive facts to people who should not have them.
Keep documents in a controlled, access-limited store with versions
Right. Control keeps sensitive details safe and shows the latest correct version.

q.q: Which finding carries the highest risk to the unit?
o: A critical flaw with a public exploit on an Internet-facing server that holds customer records and logins
Right. High likelihood and high impact together give the highest risk.
A critical flaw on a powered-off lab server that holds no data and has no network link
Impact and likelihood are both low for an isolated machine.
A low-severity flaw on a printer inside the firewall, with no data on it
Low severity, no data and no exposure make this low risk.
A medium flaw on a test box that can be reached by only one admin from one locked-down workstation
Few people can reach it, so the likelihood is low.

q.q: A unit buys cyber insurance to cover the cost of a possible breach. Which risk approach is this?
o: Risk avoidance
Avoidance means stopping the activity that causes the risk.
Risk transfer
Right. Insurance moves part of the financial loss to another party.
Risk acceptance
Acceptance means living with the risk and doing nothing about it.
Risk mitigation
Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact with controls, such as patching.

q.q: Which data most needs strong protection under a typical data classification policy?
o: The unit's internal phone list, shared only inside the building
This is internal-use data with limited harm if seen. Records with SSNs rank higher.
A draft of next month's duty roster before it is posted
A roster is low-sensitivity internal data.
The public press release about a ceremony
Already public, so there is little to protect.
Personnel records with Social Security numbers
Right. Records that identify people and can cause harm if leaked rank as sensitive.

q.q: A server's files are damaged by ransomware. The unit restores them from last night's backup. In disaster recovery terms, what type of control is the backup restore?
o: A preventive control, because it stops the attack from happening
The attack already happened, so restoring is not prevention.
A detective control, because it spots the attack when it starts
Detective controls discover events, such as alerts. A restore does not.
A corrective control, because it fixes things after the event
Right. Corrective controls restore normal operations after harm has happened.
A deterrent control, because it discourages attackers
A restore does not discourage anyone.

q.q: Which statement best describes a business continuity plan (BCP)?
o: It lists only the steps to rebuild servers after a fire or flood
That describes a disaster recovery plan, which is narrower.
It sets the firewall rules for the DMZ
Firewall rules are a technical control and not a continuity plan.
It keeps the most important business functions running during a disruption
Right. A BCP covers people, places and processes. The disaster recovery plan focuses on restoring IT systems.
It scans the network for weak passwords on a schedule
That is vulnerability or password auditing work.

q.q: Which backup practice best protects against a fire in the server room and against ransomware?
o: Keep all backups on the same server for speed
One fire or one infection would destroy data and backups together.
Keep at least one copy offsite or offline, and test restores on a regular schedule
Right. An offsite or offline copy survives local disasters and ransomware, and testing proves the backup works.
Back up once a year to a disk kept in the same room
A year-old copy loses almost everything, and the room is a single point of failure.
Skip tests, since the backup software shows a green status every night
A green status does not prove a restore will work.

q.q: What is the main job of a SIEM?
o: Collect and correlate logs and raise alerts
Right. A SIEM brings events from many sources together so analysts can see patterns.
Encrypt every file on endpoints with a key held in the cloud
Encryption is done by other tools.
Replace the firewall by blocking bad traffic at the network edge
A SIEM watches and alerts. It does not block traffic by itself.
Scan each endpoint for missing patches and install them
Patch scanning and deployment belong to other tools.

q.q: A phishing alert fires. A tool automatically checks the link against threat feeds, disables the user's session and opens a ticket, with no analyst typing. What type of tool does this?
o: A SIEM, which collects logs and shows alerts to analysts
A SIEM raises alerts. It does not run response steps by itself.
A honeypot, which lures attackers into fake systems
A honeypot is a decoy. It does not run response steps.
A VPN concentrator, which ends encrypted tunnels
A VPN protects remote links. It does not automate a response.
SOAR, which automates response steps from written playbooks
Right. Security orchestration, automation and response runs repeatable steps.

q.q: Which event should a tier 1 analyst escalate right away?
o: A domain admin account signing in from two countries within ten minutes
Right. Impossible travel on a privileged account suggests stolen credentials.
One failed password for a user who then signs in on the second try
A single typo is normal.
Antivirus signatures updated overnight on all workstations
This is routine maintenance.
A scheduled scan that finished with no findings and no errors
A clean result needs no escalation.

q.q: In the Cyber Kill Chain, at which stage does the attacker send a malicious email attachment to the target?
o: Reconnaissance
Recon is gathering information before the attack.
Command and control
This stage comes later, when the infected host calls back.
Actions on objectives
This is the last stage, when the attacker reaches the goal.
Delivery, sending the weapon to the target
Right. Delivery is the stage when the attacker sends the weapon to the victim.

q.q: Why does a team keep a chain of custody form for a seized hard drive?
o: It encrypts the drive so nobody can read it while it is stored
A form does not encrypt anything.
It replaces the need to make a forensic copy before analysis begins
A copy preserves the original. The form only tracks custody.
It records who handled the evidence and when
Right. A documented chain shows the evidence was not altered or swapped.
It proves the drive held malware at the time it was taken
A form records handling. It does not prove what was on the drive.

q.q: What is the MITRE ATT&CK matrix?
o: A catalog of public vulnerabilities, each with its own ID and score
That is closer to a vulnerability database such as CVE.
A knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques seen in real intrusions
Right. Analysts use it to describe and compare attacker behavior.
A model that links an attacker, a victim, tools and infrastructure
That describes the Diamond Model, not the ATT&CK matrix.
A list of seven stages from reconnaissance to actions on objectives
That describes the Cyber Kill Chain, not the ATT&CK matrix.

q.q: A clinic loses a laptop that holds patient records. Which framework most directly covers this data?
o: PCI DSS, the rules for payment card data
PCI DSS covers payment card data.
HIPAA, the law on patient health information
Right. HIPAA protects health information and sets breach notice duties.
FERPA, the law on student education records
FERPA covers student education records.
FISMA, the law on federal agency information systems
FISMA sets security duties for federal systems. It is not the law for patient records.

q.q: An organization holds personal data of people in the EU and learns of a breach. What does GDPR generally require?
o: Notice to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it
Right. GDPR sets a short time limit for reporting personal data breaches, where feasible.
Notice to every affected person within 24 hours, with no other step
GDPR sets 72 hours for the authority. Notice to people depends on the risk to them.
A report to the vendor within 30 days, then to the authority
The authority has to be told sooner, and a vendor is not the regulator.
Notice to the authority only if more than 10,000 people were affected
GDPR has no such size threshold for notifying the authority.

q.q: Which TWO ways can compliance rules change how a team handles an incident? (Choose two.)
o: They can require a documented record of what happened and what was done
Right. Records show the team followed the rules.
They remove the need for an incident response plan
Rules usually expect a plan, not no plan.
They let the team skip containment if a fine is paid
Fines don't replace the duty to stop the harm.
They forbid collecting any logs
Logs are normally needed for the record.
They can set who must be told and by when
Right. Rules such as HIPAA or GDPR name the people and the deadlines for notice.

q.q: In the NIST incident response lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2), which phase includes a lessons-learned meeting and a final report?
o: Preparation, building the team and its tools before anything happens
Preparation comes before any incident, with plans and training.
Detection and analysis, confirming and sizing up the event
This phase confirms and scopes the incident, not the review after it.
Containment, eradication and recovery, stopping and fixing the damage
This phase stops the harm and restores systems. The review comes after.
Post-incident activity, the review after the incident
Right. After recovery, the team reviews what happened and improves its plan.

q.q: Which activity belongs in the preparation phase of incident response?
o: Restoring servers from backup after an attack
Restoration is part of the recovery phase.
Disconnecting an infected PC from the network during an incident
That is containment, which happens during an incident.
Writing the plan, naming roles and training the team
Right. Preparation sets everything in place before an incident.
Writing a lessons-learned report once the incident has ended
Reports come after the incident, in post-incident activity.

q.q: Malware is spreading from one workstation to others in the same office. Which step comes next to limit damage?
o: Eradication, removing the malware from every system at once
Cleanup works better after the spread is stopped.
Recovery, restoring every workstation from last night's backup
Restoring before containing risks reinfection.
Post-incident activity, writing the lessons-learned report
The review comes after the incident is over.
Containment, such as isolating the affected systems
Right. Containment stops the spread before cleanup and recovery.

q.title: Read the file server's Security log
q.scenario: FS01 is a Windows file server. A monitoring alert said the server's Security log was cleared this morning. The log you have is the copy forwarded to the SIEM (central log system), so the clear did not erase it. You are authorized to review this export. Mark every line that belongs to the attack, then say what happened.
q.ticket: Alert 3304: Security log cleared on FS01 at 09:47. Review the export from 02:00 to 10:31.

lines.text: 02:00:03 4624 Logon Success user=svc_backup type=5 (service) host=FS01 src=-
lines.why: The nightly backup service starts at 02:00. A service logon at a set time is routine.

lines.text: 08:14:02 4624 Logon Success user=jlee type=2 (console) host=FS01 src=-
lines.why: A staff member signing in at the keyboard during the work day is normal.

lines.text: 09:41:10 4625 Logon Failed user=admin type=10 (RDP) src=203.0.113.45 reason=bad password
lines.why: A failed remote desktop logon from an outside address. On its own it is noise, but it starts a pattern.

lines.text: 09:41:12 4625 Logon Failed user=administrator type=10 (RDP) src=203.0.113.45 reason=bad password
lines.why: The same outside address now tries a different common account name two seconds later. That is guessing.

lines.text: 09:41:14 4625 Logon Failed user=backup type=10 (RDP) src=203.0.113.45 reason=bad password
lines.why: A third account name from the same address in four seconds. Together these lines show a password-guessing run.

lines.text: 09:41:17 4625 Logon Failed user=svc_sql type=10 (RDP) src=203.0.113.45 reason=bad password
lines.why: Next the same address tries a service account name, svc_sql.

lines.text: 09:42:01 4624 Logon Success user=svc_sql type=10 (RDP) src=203.0.113.45
lines.why: A successful remote desktop logon by the account that was just guessed, from the same outside address. The guessing worked.

lines.text: 09:44:30 4720 A user account was created: support_tmp by svc_sql
lines.why: A service account has no reason to create users. The attacker is making a new way back in.

lines.text: 09:44:52 4732 Member added to group Administrators: support_tmp by svc_sql
lines.why: The new account becomes an administrator. This is privilege escalation for persistence.

lines.text: 09:47:19 1102 The audit log was cleared by svc_sql
lines.why: Clearing the Security log is a common way to hide what just happened.

lines.text: 10:05:00 4625 Logon Failed user=mtorres type=3 src=10.1.5.22 reason=bad password
lines.why: One typo from an inside address. The next line shows the user signing in.

lines.text: 10:05:09 4624 Logon Success user=mtorres type=3 src=10.1.5.22
lines.why: The same user succeeds nine seconds later from the same inside address. This is an ordinary retry.

lines.text: 10:30:41 4624 Logon Success user=svc_backup type=5 (service) host=FS01 src=-
lines.why: A service logon by the backup account, the same pattern as at 02:00. It is routine and has no link to the attack.

ask.label: What does this log show?
opts: Password guessing from outside that worked, then a new admin account and a cleared log
A normal workday with an unlucky user who mistyped a password
A malware scan that found and removed a threat from a service account
A failed backup job that retried and then cleared its own log
ask.why: The outside address tried several account names, then signed in as svc_sql, created and promoted a new account and cleared the log. The mistyped password is from an inside user who then succeeded. No scan or backup job produces these steps.

checks.t: Listed the host's connections with netstat

checks.t: Captured traffic to the remote host with tcpdump
checks.why: A filter on that one host shows a small packet every 60 seconds. Regular beats like this are typical of a program calling home.

checks.t: Took the host off the network
checks.why: Turning off the network stops the traffic and keeps the host and its files available as evidence. The capture is best done first because it needs the link up.

checks.t: Did not scan other systems or connect out to the remote address
checks.why: Your authorization covers this workstation only. A scan of the network or contact with an outside address is out of scope and may be illegal.

checks.t: Did not delete the suspicious file or kill the process before reporting
checks.why: The file and the running process are evidence. Deleting or killing them first can erase what the incident team needs.

q.title: Order the response to ransomware on a file server
q.scenario: A file server shows locked files and a ransom note. Antivirus raised an alert twenty minutes ago on this one host. Nothing is spreading yet. Build the response in the order the NIST incident response lifecycle (SP 800-61 Rev. 2) suggests. Some ideas do not belong. Add the steps in the order they should happen.
q.ticket: INC-7731: ransomware note on FS02. The incident plan names you as first responder. Management has not yet decided anything about payment.

rules.text: Confirm the alert in the logs and find which systems are affected
rules.why: Detection and analysis comes first. You need to know it is real and how far it reaches before you act.

rules.text: Isolate the infected server from the network
rules.why: Containment stops the spread while you still have the host available. It follows confirmation, so you do not cut off a healthy system.

rules.text: Take a forensic copy of the disk and memory and log who holds it
rules.why: Evidence must be saved before cleanup changes the machine, and the chain of custody keeps it trusted.

rules.text: Remove the malware and close the weakness that let it in
rules.why: Eradication fixes the cause. Doing it after containment and the evidence copy keeps the proof and stops reinfection.

rules.text: Restore from clean backups and watch the system closely
rules.why: Recovery brings service back. It comes after the cause is removed, or the problem returns.

rules.text: Hold a lessons-learned meeting and update the plan
rules.why: The review comes at the end, when the facts are complete, and it feeds back into preparation for the next incident.

rules.text: Pay the ransom first to get the files back quickly
rules.why: Paying does not guarantee the files come back, funds attackers, and skips containment. Policy and leaders decide this, not the first responder.

rules.text: Wipe and reinstall the server before anyone looks at it
rules.why: Wiping destroys the evidence and hides how the attacker got in, so the same hole stays open.

rules.text: Post the technical details on a public forum for advice
rules.why: Public posting can leak sensitive facts. Share through the approved channels.

before.why: Confirm the scope before isolating, or you may cut off the wrong systems.
Stop the spread first, then save the evidence from the contained host.
Make the forensic copy before cleanup changes the machine.
Remove the cause before bringing the server back, or it is infected again.

last.why: The review closes the lifecycle. It uses the facts from every earlier step and improves the plan for next time.

q.title: Place the parts of a small office network
q.scenario: A small unit is building a network behind one Internet link. It hosts a public web page, lets some staff work from home and offers Wi-Fi for visitors. Place each part in the right spot. Three parts in the tray do not belong in this design.
q.ticket: Design review NR-12. Rules: nothing public touches the database, visitors stay off the inside network, and attacks are stopped at the edge where possible.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: first device after the Internet; filters traffic by rules

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: inline just behind Spot A; can drop attacks

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: public-facing; reachable from the Internet on port 443 only

slots.label: Spot D
slots.hint: ends the encrypted tunnels for staff working from home

slots.label: Spot E
slots.hint: no direct Internet route; only the inside network reaches it

slots.label: Spot F
slots.hint: visitors only; no route to the inside servers

devs.name: Edge firewall
devs.why: It is the first stop and enforces the rules for what may enter or leave. Everything below it is protected by this layer.

devs.name: Inline IPS
devs.why: An intrusion prevention system sits in the path and can drop attacks. It adds a second layer behind the firewall.

devs.name: Public web server
devs.why: The server visitors reach goes in the DMZ. If it is hit, the inside network is still behind a second barrier.

devs.name: VPN gateway
devs.why: Remote staff connect here through an encrypted tunnel, and the gateway decides what they can reach.

devs.name: Database server
devs.why: Internal data stays on an inside segment with no Internet route, reachable only from approved inside hosts.

devs.name: Guest Wi-Fi VLAN
devs.why: A separate segment keeps visitors' devices away from the inside servers, which limits how far a bad guest device could reach.

devs.name: Database server in the DMZ
devs.why: Placing private data on a public-facing segment exposes it. If the web server falls, the database is next.

devs.name: IDS on a span port
devs.why: An IDS only watches a copy of the traffic and alerts. It cannot drop an attack, which the spot needs.

devs.name: Guest Wi-Fi bridged to inside
devs.why: A bridge gives visitors a direct path to inside systems and defeats the purpose of a guest network.

q.title: Rank the weekly vulnerability scan
q.scenario: The weekly authorized scan of the unit's network finished. The team can fix only a few things before Friday. Mark every line that needs urgent action first, then say how you decide the order.
q.ticket: Scan job VS-0415, approved by the system owner. Maintenance window: Friday night.

lines.text: web01  DMZ  Internet-facing  CRITICAL 9.8  Remote code execution in web framework  Public exploit available  Holds customer records
lines.why: An easy-to-reach flaw that gives full control, with a public exploit and sensitive data behind it. Highest likelihood and highest impact.

lines.text: vpn01  Edge  Internet-facing  HIGH 8.8  Login bypass  Listed as exploited in the wild by a national alert
lines.why: Attackers are using this flaw now, and the device is the front door for remote staff. Severity plus active exploitation moves it to the top.

lines.text: fs03  Inside  CRITICAL 9.0  SMBv1 enabled, unsupported OS, shared by 200 users  Reachable from guest VLAN
lines.why: The old protocol and OS can't be patched, and the guest network can reach it. Many users depend on it, so impact is high.

lines.why: The score is high, but the machine is off, isolated and holds nothing. The risk is low, so fix it on a normal schedule or retire it.

lines.text: prn03  Inside  LOW 3.1  Printer firmware version disclosed in banner
lines.why: A small information leak on an inside printer. Worth fixing later, not urgent.

lines.text: wiki01  Inside  MEDIUM 5.3  Missing HTTP security header  Staff login required
lines.why: A medium weakness that needs a login to reach. It goes in the regular patch cycle.

lines.text: wks-114  Inside  MEDIUM 5.0  Outdated PDF reader  Auto-update scheduled tonight
lines.why: A fix is already scheduled for tonight, so no extra action is needed.

lines.text: dev-laptop7  Inside  INFO  Self-signed certificate on a test web page
lines.why: An informational note about a test page. It does not need action.

ask.label: What is the best way to rank findings?
opts: By the severity score alone, highest number first
By severity together with exposure, active exploitation and the value of the data
By the order the scanner printed them, top to bottom
By which fix is quickest, to clear the most lines
ask.why: Risk is likelihood times impact. A critical score on an isolated, powered-off lab box matters less than a high score on an exposed server that attackers already use. Score alone, print order and speed ignore that.
